etymology: Hebrew Layish, “a lion,” the old name of the northern city later called Dan.
biblical_def: Laish was a city in the far north of the land, near the headwaters of the Jordan, inhabited by a careless people who dwelt “quiet and secure, after the manner of the Zidonians,” far from any that might trouble them (Judg 18:7). When the tribe of Dan, unable to possess its allotted coast, sent men to seek a place to dwell, the spies marked Laish as a fat and unguarded prize; and six hundred armed Danites went up, smote the people with the edge of the sword, and burnt the city with fire (Judg 18:27). They rebuilt it and called it Dan, after the name of their father (Judg 18:29); it is also named Leshem in the book of Joshua (Josh 19:47). But the conquest of Laish was no act of faith. The Danites carried with them the stolen graven image of Micah and the renegade Levite, and set up idolatry in the new city, which continued “all the time that the house of God was in Shiloh” (Judg 18:31). Thus Dan, the northernmost city of Israel, became from its founding a seat of false worship, and later one of Jeroboam’s two golden calves was placed there. Laish stands as a warning that men may gain a possession and yet defile it from the first stone with the worship of an idol.
webster_summary: The northern city, formerly Laish or Leshem, taken by the Danites and renamed Dan; a seat of idolatry from its founding.

It is also called Leshem in the inheritance of Dan (Josh 19:47).
There the Danites set up Micah’s graven image, defiling the city from the first (Judg 18:31).

corruption_summary: A place-name, not a contested doctrine; its lesson is that a possession seized for self and defiled with idolatry is cursed from the first.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Danites’ conquest of Laish was not obedience but self-will: they sought ease and a fat land, took it by force apart from God’s leading, and brought a stolen idol with them. A people may prosper outwardly and yet build their house upon false worship; such a foundation is rotten however fair the city.

Laish, renamed Dan, became a fountain of idolatry for all Israel, for there Jeroboam set one of his golden calves. The lesson is that sin planted at the founding of a thing spreads through its whole history. What the Danites carried up to Laish poisoned the worship of the nation for centuries; small compromise at the beginning becomes great corruption in the end.
roots_summary: The name means “a lion,” one of several Hebrew words for that beast, here fixed to the old city of Dan.

Laish teaches that quiet and security without God are no true safety, for the careless city fell in a day.
What was carried up to Laish defiled a nation, proving that small compromise breeds great corruption.

etymology: Hebrew Dor, perhaps “dwelling” or “generation,” a royal Canaanite city on the Mediterranean coast.
biblical_def: Dor was a royal Canaanite city on the seacoast south of Mount Carmel, called also Naphoth-dor, “the heights of Dor.” Its king was among those that gathered to Jabin king of Hazor in the great northern confederacy against Israel, and he perished with the rest when the LORD delivered them into Israel’s hand (Josh 11:2; 12:23). The city fell within the inheritance of Manasseh, though it lay in the territory of Asher and Issachar (Josh 17:11). Yet Manasseh could not drive out the inhabitants, “but the Canaanites would dwell in that land” (Judg 1:27); the strong coastal city was only made tributary, never fully cleansed. In Solomon’s reign Dor and its region formed one of the twelve districts that provided victuals for the king’s household, governed by the son of Abinadab who had Solomon’s daughter to wife (1Ki 4:11). Dor is remembered chiefly as one of the places where Israel failed to complete the conquest, leaving the Canaanite in the land to become a snare. It witnesses that a half-finished obedience leaves a thorn that will prick the people for generations.
webster_summary: A royal Canaanite seacoast city south of Carmel; in Manasseh’s lot, but its Canaanites were never driven out.

corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson is that an unfinished obedience leaves a Canaanite in the land.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the danger of partial conquest. Manasseh defeated the king of Dor but failed to dispossess the people, choosing tribute over obedience. So the believer who spares a besetting sin, making peace with what God commanded him to put to death, leaves a thorn that will wound him and his children after him.

Dor stands among the long list of Judges 1 where the tribes “could not” drive out the Canaanites — a could-not that the narrative shows to be a would-not, a failure of faith and resolve rather than mere weakness. The LORD had promised the land; the fault lay in Israel’s slackness, not in any lack on God’s part.
roots_summary: The name may mean “dwelling” or “generation,” fixed to a coastal stronghold known for its heights.

etymology: Hebrew Yoqne’am, perhaps “the people laments” or “possessed by the people,” a royal city by Mount Carmel.
biblical_def: Jokneam, called Jokneam of Carmel, was a royal Canaanite city at the foot of Mount Carmel near the border of Zebulun. Its king was one of the thirty-one kings whom Joshua and the children of Israel smote on the west side of Jordan when the land was taken (Josh 12:22). The river that ran before Jokneam marked part of the border of Zebulun’s inheritance (Josh 19:11). When the Levites received their cities, Jokneam in Zebulun was given with its suburbs to the families of the children of Merari, the keepers of the boards, bars, and pillars of the tabernacle (Josh 21:34). Thus a city once ruled by a Canaanite king became a dwelling of the Levites, set apart for the service of the LORD and the teaching of His law. Jokneam appears but briefly in Scripture, yet its history traces the pattern of the whole conquest: a heathen stronghold overthrown, its land apportioned to the tribes, and a portion given over to those who ministered before God. It is a quiet token that the LORD takes the strongholds of the nations and turns them to the uses of His worship.
webster_summary: A royal Canaanite city by Mount Carmel on Zebulun’s border, given to the Levites of Merari’s family.

corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson is that God turns the strongholds of the heathen into dwellings for His servants.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the design by which a Canaanite royal city became a Levitical town. What had been a seat of idolatry was given to the keepers of the tabernacle, that the law of the LORD might be taught where false gods were once served. God delights to take what was raised against Him and consecrate it to His worship.

Jokneam also displays the orderliness of the conquest. The land was not seized by greed but divided by lot under the hand of God, and a portion was set apart for the Levites among every tribe, so that no part of Israel should be without the presence and teaching of those who ministered before the LORD. The provision for worship was woven into the very map of the inheritance.

etymology: Hebrew Shimron, “a watch” or “guardpost,” a royal city of the north in the lot of Zebulun.
biblical_def: Shimron, called also Shimron-meron, was a royal Canaanite city in the north of the land. When Jabin king of Hazor heard of Israel’s advance, he gathered a vast confederacy against them, and the king of Shimron was among those he summoned (Josh 11:1). With the kings of Madon, Achshaph, and the rest, this multitude pitched at the waters of Merom, “even as the sand that is upon the sea shore in multitude” (Josh 11:4); yet the LORD delivered them all into the hand of Israel, who smote them until none remained (Josh 11:8). The king of Shimron-meron is duly numbered in the roll of thirty-one kings overthrown west of Jordan (Josh 12:20). The city itself afterward fell within the inheritance of Zebulun (Josh 19:15). Shimron, “the watch,” could not watch against the God of Israel; its name promised vigilance, but no guardpost of the heathen can stand when the LORD has decreed a land to His people. It takes its small place in Scripture as one stone in the great heap of kings whom God cast down to give Israel rest in the land of promise.
webster_summary: A royal Canaanite city of the north, in Zebulun’s lot, whose king joined Jabin’s confederacy and fell.

corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson is that no watchpost of the heathen can stand against the decree of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the multitude and chariots of the northern kings, gathered like the sand of the sea, availed nothing when the LORD had purposed to give the land to Israel. Shimron’s very name means “a watch,” yet it could not keep watch against the Almighty. The arm of flesh fails where God has spoken.

Shimron also rebukes the trust in numbers and arms that marked the Canaanite league. They came with horses and chariots very many; Israel had neither, but had the promise of God. The battle was the LORD’s, and He hamstrung their horses and burned their chariots with fire (Josh 11:6–9), that His people might learn to lean on Him and not on the strength of war.
roots_summary: The name means “a watch” or “guardpost,” an irony for a city that could not guard itself against the LORD.

etymology: Hebrew Akshaph, perhaps “sorcery” or “enchantment,” a royal city in the border of Asher.
biblical_def: Achshaph was a royal Canaanite city in the north, lying within the borders of the tribe of Asher. Its king answered the summons of Jabin king of Hazor and joined the great confederacy of northern kings who gathered at the waters of Merom to fight against Israel (Josh 11:1). When the LORD delivered that host into Israel’s hand, the king of Achshaph was slain among the rest, and his name is written in the roll of the thirty-one kings overthrown in the conquest (Josh 12:20). The city is afterward named among the bounds of Asher’s inheritance (Josh 19:25). The meaning of its name, bound up with sorcery or enchantment, fits the dark religion of the Canaanites, whose abominations of divination and witchcraft were among the reasons the LORD cast them out before Israel (Deut 18:9–12). Achshaph thus appears as one more heathen stronghold given over to judgment, its enchantments powerless against the word of the living God. It teaches that the spells and divinations of the nations cannot turn aside the purpose of the LORD, who gave the land to the seed of Abraham according to His oath.
webster_summary: A royal Canaanite city in Asher’s border whose king joined Jabin’s league; its name suggests sorcery.

The city is named among the borders of Asher (Josh 19:25).

corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson is that the enchantments of the heathen cannot turn aside the purpose of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the sorceries woven into the name of Achshaph, like all the divinations of Canaan, were powerless against the LORD. He cast out the nations for their witchcraft and gave their land to His people; no enchantment could shield the city from the judgment that the abominations of the Amorite had ripened to receive.

Achshaph reminds the reader that the conquest was, among other things, the execution of a long-deferred sentence upon a people sunk in occult abomination. The LORD is patient, but He is not mocked; the iniquity of the Amorites came to the full, and the city of enchantments fell. The same God still forbids His people every traffic with divination and the dark arts.
roots_summary: The name is linked to sorcery or enchantment, fitting the dark religion of the Canaanite cities.

etymology: Hebrew Madon, perhaps “strife” or “contention,” a royal city of the north under King Jobab.
biblical_def: Madon was a royal Canaanite city in the north, ruled by Jobab, who was the first king summoned when Jabin of Hazor raised the great confederacy against Israel (Josh 11:1). With the kings of Shimron, Achshaph, and many more, Jobab of Madon led out his host to the waters of Merom, a multitude with horses and chariots very many, set on driving the people of God back into the wilderness. But the LORD said to Joshua, “Be not afraid because of them: for to morrow about this time will I deliver them up all slain before Israel” (Josh 11:6); and so it came to pass, for Israel fell upon them and smote them until none was left remaining. The king of Madon is recorded in the roll of the thirty-one kings whom Joshua overthrew (Josh 12:19). Madon’s name, bound up with strife and contention, fits a king who stirred up war against the LORD’s inheritance. The city teaches that those who gather themselves together to contend against God’s people gather only to their own destruction; the strife they raise recoils upon their own heads.
webster_summary: A royal Canaanite city ruled by King Jobab, first summoned to Jabin’s northern league against Israel.

corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson is that those who raise strife against God’s people gather to their own ruin.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the assurance the LORD gave Joshua: “Be not afraid because of them.” Though the kings gathered in multitudes against Israel, the outcome was settled in heaven before the battle was joined. The people of God need not fear the confederacies of the nations, for the LORD has appointed their end.

Madon’s name, “strife,” fits a king who stirred up war against the inheritance of God. Scripture warns that the counsel of the heathen against the LORD and against His anointed is vain; “he that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh” (Ps 2:4). The strife raised against God’s people recoils upon those who raise it.

etymology: Hebrew Akko, a coastal city of Asher; called Ptolemais in the New Testament era.
biblical_def: Accho was a city and harbour on the Mediterranean coast within the lot of the tribe of Asher, north of Mount Carmel by the bay that bears its name. It is named in the sad catalogue of the first chapter of Judges as one of the cities whose Canaanite inhabitants Asher failed to drive out: “Neither did Asher drive out the inhabitants of Accho, nor the inhabitants of Zidon” and others, but the Asherites dwelt among the Canaanites of the land (Judg 1:31–32). Thus, like so many of the coastal tribes, Asher made peace with the people it was charged to dispossess, and the unconquered city remained. In the days of the apostles the place was known as Ptolemais, and there the apostle Paul, returning from his third journey, landed and saluted the brethren and abode with them one day (Acts 21:7). Accho therefore joins the Old Testament record of incomplete obedience to a New Testament glimpse of the gospel reaching the same coast. It witnesses both to Israel’s failure to finish the conquest and to the wider mercy by which, in the fulness of time, the word of Christ came to the very places the law had left unsubdued.
webster_summary: A coastal city in Asher’s lot, never cleared of its Canaanites; the Ptolemais where Paul landed (Acts 21:7).

corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson joins Israel’s unfinished obedience to the wider reach of the gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the danger of dwelling among what God commanded to be driven out. Asher did not drive out the men of Accho but settled among them, and so the tribe was slowly conformed to the people it should have dispossessed. The believer who makes his home among the world’s idols, instead of putting them away, is shaped by them in the end.

Yet Accho also shows a gracious turn. The coast the law left unsubdued was reached at last by the gospel, when Paul greeted the brethren at Ptolemais. Where Israel’s obedience failed, the mercy of God in Christ went further, gathering a people to Himself even in the cities the old conquest never cleansed.

etymology: Hebrew Qedesh, “a sanctuary” or “holy place,” the city of refuge in the hill country of Naphtali.
biblical_def: Kedesh in Galilee, in mount Naphtali, was a royal Canaanite city overthrown in the conquest (Josh 12:22) and afterward appointed one of the six cities of refuge, whither the manslayer might flee from the avenger of blood (Josh 20:7). It was also given to the Levites of the family of Gershon as a dwelling and pasture (Josh 21:32). Kedesh was the home of Barak the son of Abinoam, whom Deborah the prophetess called out to deliver Israel from Jabin and his captain Sisera; there Barak gathered ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun to mount Tabor (Judg 4:6, 10). Near Kedesh dwelt Heber the Kenite, in whose tent Sisera fled and fell by the hand of Jael. In the latter days of the northern kingdom, Tiglath-pileser of Assyria took Kedesh with the rest of the land of Naphtali and carried the people captive (2Ki 15:29). The name Kedesh means “sanctuary,” and the city was indeed a sanctuary in a double sense: a refuge for the manslayer under the law, and a token of the greater refuge to which sinners flee for safety. It pictures the mercy of God that provides a hiding-place for the guilty who lay hold on His appointed shelter.
webster_summary: A city of refuge and Levitical town in mount Naphtali; the home of Barak the judge.

Josh 21:32
And out of the tribe of Naphtali, Kedesh in Galilee with her suburbs, to be a city of refuge for the slayer; and Hammothdor with her suburbs, and Kartan with her suburbs; three cities.
corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson is the mercy of the appointed refuge for the guilty who flee to it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the gospel pictured in the city of refuge. Kedesh, the “sanctuary,” stood open for the manslayer who fled from the avenger of blood, that he might live within its walls until the death of the high priest. So the sinner, pursued by the law’s just sentence, flees to Christ, the true refuge, and is safe in Him; the writer to the Hebrews speaks of fleeing for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us (Heb 6:18).

Kedesh also reminds the reader that the city of refuge was no shelter for the murderer who slew with hatred, but only for the one who killed unawares. The refuge was a place of mercy ordered by justice, not a denial of justice. So the salvation that is in Christ is full mercy to the penitent, but it does not abolish the righteousness of God; it satisfies it in the death of the great High Priest.
roots_summary: The name means “a sanctuary” or “holy place,” fitting a city set apart as a refuge.
roots_lines: Kedesh — Hebrew Qedesh, “a sanctuary, a holy place.”
The root qadash means to be set apart or holy.
It is called Kedesh in Galilee and Kedesh-naphtali to mark its region.
It was both a city of refuge and a Levitical town.
The sanctuary-city pictures the refuge sinners find in Christ.
usage: Like the manslayer fleeing to Kedesh, the sinner flees for refuge to lay hold on the hope set before him.
Kedesh teaches that the refuge of God is mercy ordered by justice, not justice denied.
From Kedesh came Barak, called by the word of the LORD to deliver Israel from her oppressor.

etymology: Hebrew Yavne’el, “God causeth to build” or “God will build,” the name of two border towns.
biblical_def: Jabneel was the name of two towns that marked the borders of the tribal inheritances. One lay on the boundary of Judah toward the sea, between the mountain of Baalah and the great sea, in the list of Judah’s coastal landmarks (Josh 15:11); this town was later known as Jabneh or Jamnia. The other Jabneel was a border town of Naphtali in the north, named among the fenced cities of that tribe near the sea of Chinnereth (Josh 19:33). The name itself is a confession of faith woven into the map of the land: “God causeth to build,” or “God will build.” Every boundary stone and border town of Israel was set by the hand of the LORD who divided the inheritance to the tribes by lot, so that the very names of the towns bore witness to the God who planted His people in the land. Jabneel, small and little mentioned, stands among the borders as a quiet reminder that it is God who builds the house and the city; except the LORD build it, they labour in vain that build it (Ps 127:1). The bounds of Israel were not the work of men’s ambition but the gift and building of God.
webster_summary: A border town, by one of two sites, whose name confesses that God builds; on the bounds of Judah and of Naphtali.
webster_full: JABNEEL, the name of two border towns in the tribal inheritances.
One marked the border of Judah toward the sea, later called Jabneh (Josh 15:11).
The other was a fenced city on the border of Naphtali (Josh 19:33).
Its name signifies “God causeth to build” or “God will build.”
It stands among the boundary marks of the land divided by lot.
scriptures: Josh 15:11

And the border went out unto the side of Ekron northward: and the border was drawn to Shicron, and passed along to mount Baalah, and went out unto Jabneel; and the goings out of the border were at the sea.
Josh 19:33
And their coast was from Heleph, from Allon to Zaanannim, and Adami, Nekeb, and Jabneel, unto Lakum; and the outgoings thereof were at Jordan:
Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
Josh 14:5
As the LORD commanded Moses, so the children of Israel did, and they divided the land.
corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson is that God Himself builds the house and the city of His people.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is sealed in the name: “God will build.” The borders of Israel were not drawn by the cunning of men but apportioned by the LORD through the lot, so that the very towns confessed His hand. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it; the prosperity of a people, a family, or a church is the gift of God, not the achievement of human strength.

Jabneel, little remembered, also teaches that no part of God’s ordering is too small for His care. He numbered the border stones and named the obscure towns of His people. The same God who builds the unnamed places builds the lives of the humblest of His saints, whose names are written in heaven though forgotten on earth.
roots_summary: The name joins a verb “to build” with El, “God,” confessing that God is the builder.
roots_lines: Jabneel — Hebrew Yavne’el, “God causeth to build.”
The element El (“God”) closes many Hebrew names.
The verb-root banah means to build or establish.
One Jabneel lay in Judah, another in Naphtali.
The border-town’s name confesses the God who builds His people’s house.
usage: Like Jabneel, every house and city of God’s people is built by His hand, not by human strength.
Jabneel teaches that except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it.
The obscure border-town confesses by its very name the God who orders even the smallest things.

etymology: Hebrew Kinnereth, perhaps from kinnor, “a harp,” from the harp-like shape of the lake; a city and the sea of the same name.
biblical_def: Chinnereth was both a fenced city in the tribe of Naphtali and the name of the inland sea on whose shore it stood, the great lake known in the New Testament as the sea of Galilee or Gennesaret (Josh 19:35). The “sea of Chinnereth” is named as a landmark in the bounds of the land, for the eastern border ran down to its side (Num 34:11), and the inheritance east of Jordan reached unto the edge of the sea of Chinneroth (Josh 13:27). The name is thought to come from the harp, perhaps for the shape of the lake. Though Chinnereth the city is little mentioned, the waters that bore its name became, in the fulness of time, the most hallowed lake in all the earth: for upon the sea of Galilee the Lord Jesus walked, stilled the storm, called fishermen to be fishers of men, and taught the multitudes from a boat near the shore. Thus the Old Testament “sea of Chinnereth” and the New Testament “sea of Galilee” are the same waters, and the quiet border-name of Naphtali became the scene of the mightiest works of the incarnate Son of God. Chinnereth witnesses how the LORD prepares, long beforehand, the very places where He will display His glory.
webster_summary: A fenced city in Naphtali and the inland sea of the same name, known later as the sea of Galilee.
webster_full: CHINNERETH, a fenced city of Naphtali and the inland sea on whose shore it lay.
The sea of Chinnereth marked the eastern border of the land (Num 34:11).
The trans-Jordan inheritance reached to the edge of the sea of Chinneroth (Josh 13:27).
The city is named among the fenced towns of Naphtali (Josh 19:35).
Its waters are the sea of Galilee or Gennesaret of the New Testament.
scriptures: And the coast shall go down from Shepham to Riblah, on the east side of Ain; and the border shall descend, and shall reach unto the side of the sea of Chinnereth eastward:
Josh 19:35
And the fenced cities are Ziddim, Zer, and Hammath, Rakkath, and Chinnereth,
Josh 13:27

And in the valley, Betharam, and Bethnimrah, and Succoth, and Zaphon, the rest of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon, Jordan and his border, even unto the edge of the sea of Chinnereth on the other side Jordan eastward.
Deut 3:17
The plain also, and Jordan, and the coast thereof, from Chinnereth even unto the sea of the plain, even the salt sea, under Ashdothpisgah eastward.
corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson is that God prepares long beforehand the places where He will show His glory.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the providence that runs from Chinnereth to Galilee. The same waters that the book of Numbers names as a mere border-mark became the scene of Christ’s walking on the sea, His stilling of the tempest, and His calling of the apostles. God appointed those shores ages before His Son trod them; nothing in the map of redemption is accidental.

Chinnereth also teaches that the obscure may be made glorious by the presence of the LORD. A little fenced town of Naphtali gave its name to the lake where the Word made flesh displayed His power over wind and wave. The places men pass over without notice may be the very places God has chosen to honour with the manifestation of His Son.
roots_summary: The name is linked to the harp, kinnor, perhaps for the curving shape of the lake.
roots_lines: Chinnereth — Hebrew Kinnereth, perhaps from kinnor, “a harp.”
The name was borne by both a city and the inland sea.
It is also spelled Chinneroth in the plural form.
The sea of Chinnereth is the sea of Galilee of the Gospels.
The harp-shaped lake became the stage of Christ’s mighty works.
usage: Like Chinnereth made Galilee, the LORD prepares long beforehand the places where He will reveal His glory.
Chinnereth teaches that the obscure is made glorious by the presence of Christ.
The border-sea of Naphtali became the lake where the Son of God walked upon the waves.
